chapters.title: Knaves, Fools, Villains, and Hypocrites: How Do They Live with Themselves?
chapters.sourcePressure: The opening puzzle is how people can acknowledge damage while protecting a decent self-image; the source centers on passive non-apology language, self-justification versus lying, and the way agency disappears when ownership feels dangerous.
chapters.coreMove: Hear the sentence where ownership disappears, then restore the actor before the story protects the self too well.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating self-justification as obvious lying by bad people, instead of a sincere identity defense ordinary people use after harm.
mustNotDriftInto: communication tips detached from identity threat

chapters.title: Cognitive Dissonance: The Engine of Self-justification
chapters.sourcePressure: This mechanism chapter explains cognitive dissonance as the pressure created when belief, behavior, and self-image collide; the source supports the smoker contradiction, Leon Festinger's failed-prophecy group, and post-choice hardening.
chapters.coreMove: When contradiction hurts, identify whether the person is changing behavior or merely changing the story that makes the behavior livable.
chapters.commonMisread: Reducing cognitive dissonance to ordinary discomfort or inconsistency, without showing how relief can outrun truth after commitment.

chapters.title: Pride and Prejudice . . . and Other Blind Spots
chapters.sourcePressure: The chapter moves from dissonance into naive realism, bias blind spots, and prejudice; the source stresses that people experience their own view as reality while seeing the opponent as distorted.
chapters.coreMove: Treat your own certainty as one perspective to inspect, not the neutral place from which everyone else is judged.
chapters.commonMisread: Turning blind spots into a lecture about other people's prejudice rather than the felt innocence of one's own perception.

chapters.title: Memory, the Self-justifying Historian
chapters.sourcePressure: The chapter treats memory as reconstruction rather than neutral recording; the source supports conflicting recollections, confidence without accuracy, and Anthony Greenwald's "totalitarian ego" metaphor.
chapters.coreMove: Before trusting a vivid memory, ask what present innocence the memory is helping protect.
chapters.commonMisread: Making the chapter a generic warning that memory is fallible, rather than showing memory as an identity-protecting reconstruction.

chapters.title: Good Intentions, Bad Science: The Closed Loop of Clinical Judgment
chapters.sourcePressure: The chapter critiques clinical judgment when intuition and benevolent identity become a closed loop; the source emphasizes science as error exposure, arrogance control, and the danger of suggestive interviewing.
chapters.coreMove: Turn a confident helping story into a testable hypothesis before good intentions seal the loop.
chapters.commonMisread: Attacking therapy, clinicians, or expertise broadly instead of targeting untested confirmation loops inside helping work.

chapters.title: Law and Disorder
chapters.sourcePressure: The legal-system chapter shows self-justification under coercive power: early guilt decisions, Reid-style interrogation pressure, confession over-weighting, and post-conviction resistance to innocence evidence.
chapters.coreMove: Slow the jump from suspicion to certainty before the system starts treating correction as an attack on itself.
chapters.commonMisread: Casting the legal problem as a few corrupt officials rather than ordinary self-justification magnified by authority, reputation, and institutional stakes.

chapters.title: Love's Assassin: Self-justification in Marriage
chapters.sourcePressure: The marriage chapter applies self-justification to intimate conflict: people explain their own bad behavior by circumstance and their partner's by character, then store grievance as proof.
chapters.coreMove: Translate one permanent indictment back into the specific situation before the argument becomes a trial of the other person's character.
chapters.commonMisread: Turning the chapter into generic relationship advice, apology scripts, or equal-blame smoothing instead of attribution asymmetry and stored grievance.

chapters.title: Wounds, Rifts, and Wars
chapters.sourcePressure: The group-conflict chapter scales self-justification into us-versus-them thinking, selective collective memory, grievance as identity, retaliation loops, and loyalty costs around self-examination.
chapters.coreMove: Preserve the reality of a wound without turning innocence into group property that licenses the next harm.
chapters.commonMisread: Equating all harms, flattening historical injuries, or jumping to conflict-resolution optimism instead of showing how grievance becomes self-renewing identity.

chapters.title: Letting Go and Owning Up
chapters.sourcePressure: The final chapter closes the arc with apology, repair, and conditions for real ownership; the source contrasts image-saving regret language with clear responsibility and treats letting go as neither forgetting nor excusing.
chapters.coreMove: Make dignity mean surviving an unflattering truth and acting under it, rather than staying exonerated.
chapters.commonMisread: Turning owning up into a nicer apology script or turning letting go into pressure on the harmed person to forget.
